prompt: Explain why the internal energy of a fixed mass of an ideal gas depends only on its thermodynamic temperature.

mark_scheme.criterion: States that there are no intermolecular forces between molecules (except during collisions), so intermolecular potential energy is zero (internal energy is entirely kinetic).
States that the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules is directly proportional to thermodynamic temperature (E_K = (3/2) kT), so total internal energy U = (3/2) NkT depends only on T.

hints: Recall what components make up the internal energy of any system.
Why is the potential energy component zero in an ideal gas, and how does the kinetic energy component depend on temperature?
solution: Internal energy is the sum of the random distribution of kinetic and potential energies of the molecules of a system. In an ideal gas, there are no intermolecular forces between molecules, so the intermolecular potential energy is strictly zero. The internal energy is therefore purely translational kinetic energy. Because the average translational kinetic energy per molecule is directly proportional to thermodynamic temperature (E_K = (3/2) kT), the total internal energy of a fixed mass of gas depends solely on its thermodynamic temperature.
teacher_walkthrough: First point: Intermolecular potential energy is zero because there are no intermolecular forces.
Second point: Translational kinetic energy is directly proportional to thermodynamic temperature T (E_K = 3/2 kT).
Therefore, total internal energy depends exclusively on T.
